archetype.name: Playoff Team (defense-first)
archetype.definition: A Seattle side whose league-best-caliber defense and strong special teams carry a below-average, turnover-prone offense, good enough to win most weeks and better than its 4-3 suggests.

report.headline: An elite defense lost three close games to giveaways, not to better opponents.
report.take:
This is the 2025 Seahawks defense still showing up. Last year Mike Macdonald's unit led the league in EPA allowed at -0.111. This year it sits second at -0.115, allows the fewest yards per game in the league, and gets off the field on third down as well as anyone (28%, 2nd). It erases the big play: no defense allows fewer explosive passes, and its deep-pass EPA allowed is the best in the league. Add special teams ranked 3rd in EPA per game and an aggressive fourth-down approach, and you have a team that should rarely be in a game it can't win.

The offense is the problem, and the turnovers are the main way it hurts. The offense has 13 giveaways across seven games, and the defense has taken the ball back nearly enough to cancel them out (turnover differential of -1). The giveaways clustered in the wrong games. All three losses, to Washington, San Francisco and Denver, came in Drew Lock starts with three or four turnovers each, and all three were one-score games. In Sam Darnold's two starts the offense turned it over once in total and put up positive passing EPA both times, including 12.2 in the 20-3 win over Kansas City. The point differential says 4.5 wins, so the record is a little behind the play, not ahead of it.

The numbers also hide a structural flaw. The offensive line allows pressure more often than any line in the league (27.3%), and the run game is 29th in EPA despite respectable box-score yardage. Seattle still runs more than almost anyone, with a pass rate 7 points under expected, 28th. Some of that is game script from playing with leads behind a great defense. Some of it is a stubborn identity that costs efficiency, and the team converts short yardage at the worst rate in the league. The red-zone TD rate allowed (78.6%, 30th) looks like an ugly blemish, but it is the kind of small-sample number that tends to settle for a defense that gives up this little elsewhere.

With Lock out and Darnold back under center, the turnover tap should tighten. The defense looks real and repeatable, since it held up across consecutive seasons. The ceiling depends on whether a leaky line can protect long enough, with Charles Cross doubtful, for a passing game that needs time to throw (3.0 seconds, 5th longest).

strengths.title: A defense that erases explosives
strengths.body: Seattle ranks 2nd in EPA allowed and 1st in deep-pass EPA allowed, so offenses have to string together long drives against a unit that also gets home with pressure (27.2%, 4th). This held across two seasons under the same staff, so it is not a hot streak. Expect it to stay top-five.

strengths.title: Third-down and pressure stops
strengths.body: Opponents convert only 28% of third downs, 2nd in the league, and Seattle's QB-hit rate on defense ranks 3rd. This is why points allowed stay low even when the offense hands over short fields. It is a schematic and personnel strength that should hold.

strengths.title: Hidden yards on special teams
strengths.body: Special teams add 4.01 EPA per game, 3rd in the league. Combined with a staff that goes for it on fourth down at the top rate in the league, Seattle squeezes extra points out of possessions. In a season of one-score games, that margin matters.

concerns.title: Pass protection is the league's worst
concerns.body: Seattle allows pressure on 27.3% of dropbacks, last in the league, and its QB-hit rate allowed ranks 30th. Pairing that with long developing throws invites sacks: five apiece in the San Francisco and Denver losses. With the left tackle hurt, this is a real flaw, not noise.

concerns.title: Giveaways decided every loss
concerns.body: The offense has 13 turnovers. Each loss came with three or more, peaking at four against San Francisco. Most of them came during Lock's stretch, so Darnold's return should cut the rate, but the pressure problem keeps the risk alive.

concerns.title: A run-first offense that can't run
concerns.body: Seattle runs well above expectation (pass rate 7 points under expected, 28th) with a ground game that is 29th in EPA and last in short-yardage conversion. Rushing yards look fine in the box scores because the team often plays from ahead. On a per-play basis, the commitment is costing the offense.

trend.note: Seattle opened 2-0 behind the defense, then the offense sank through Lock's middle stretch with negative passing EPA in three straight games and two narrow losses. Darnold's return produced the most complete win of the year, 20-3 over Kansas City.

nextGame.headline: Darnold's deep shots against a Bears defense that bleeds explosives
nextGame.body:
Chicago arrives 5-2, but the profile is thinner than the record. Its point differential trails its wins by more than a game (1.12 wins over expected), and its defense ranks 15th in EPA. That unit is excellent underneath and on third down (26.1%, 1st) but gives up the deep ball worse than anyone (deep EPA allowed 32nd, explosive pass rate 30th). Ben Johnson's offense moves the ball, 3rd in yards per game, and controls the clock better than any team. That will test how far Seattle's bend-but-don't-break defense can bend. The Book has Seattle -3 at home with a 46.5 total.

Availability tilts both ways. Seattle goes with Darnold, since Lock (elbow) is out, but likely without left tackle Charles Cross, who is doubtful with a high ankle sprain. That is a big loss for the league's most-pressured line. Linebacker Drake Thomas is also out, Rashid Shaheed is questionable with positive early news, and rookie back Jadarian Price is set to be designated for return. Chicago has Caleb Williams back under center for a second straight week. It is missing linebacker T.J. Edwards, running back Kyle Monangai and safety Anthony Johnson Jr., has tight end Cole Kmet on IR, and cornerback Malik Muhammad II is questionable with a toe injury.

waysToWin.title: Hit the deep shots Chicago allows
waysToWin.body: Chicago's defense is 5th against short passes and last against deep ones. The way through it is vertical, not underneath. Darnold had his best game in the last start, and if Shaheed plays and Muhammad sits, Smith-Njigba and the outside receivers should find chunk plays. That only works if protection holds long enough.

waysToWin.title: Attack the middle with Barner and backs
waysToWin.body: Chicago ranks 27th in EPA allowed to tight ends and 31st to lead backs, and it is now without T.J. Edwards at linebacker. Quick throws to AJ Barner and the backs also double as a pressure release for a line missing Cross.

waysToWin.title: Make Chicago drive the long field
waysToWin.body: Seattle's defense kills explosives and third downs. Chicago is down its tight end and a running back. If the Bears have to go 75 yards in small chunks against a top-two third-down defense, drives will stall. Seattle's ball-control edge then flips to the defense.

waysToLose.title: The Bears' rush beats a patched line
waysToLose.body: Chicago generates pressure at the 3rd-best rate and sacks quarterbacks at the 3rd-best rate. Seattle allows pressure more than anyone and likely plays without Cross. Five-sack games produced two of the losses, and a repeat stalls the deep shots that are the clearest path to points.

waysToLose.title: Third-down stalls and short-yardage failures
waysToLose.body: Chicago owns the league's best third-down defense, and Seattle is last in short-yardage conversion. Drives that die at the sticks waste the defense's work. If that is paired with another multi-turnover game, this becomes a fourth one-score loss.

waysToLose.title: Chicago lives underneath and on the clock
waysToLose.body: Seattle's one soft spot is short passing (21st in EPA allowed). Drake Thomas's absence thins the linebackers who cover that area. Chicago leads the league in time of possession and could methodically shorten the game, leaving Seattle's run-heavy offense too few possessions to catch up.

nextGame.watch: How Seattle protects Darnold without Cross: whether it buys enough time for shots at Chicago's 32nd-ranked deep defense, or gets forced into the short game where the Bears are strong.

restOfSeason.body:
The defense and special teams look like the sustainable core, and the schedule ahead is forgiving. Arizona, Las Vegas, Philadelphia, Dallas's 30th-ranked defense and a .500-ish Carolina are all on the slate, with San Francisco away and two Rams games as the stiff tests. With Darnold back, the turnover rate that drove all three losses should come down. The one-score coin flips that went against Seattle should even out somewhat, given a record already slightly behind its differential.

What won't fix itself is the line. A pressure rate this high caps the offense and keeps sacks and strip-sacks in play, especially while Cross is out. The run game should not be expected to improve much. The red-zone TD rate allowed, though, should drift toward normal, which trims points allowed further. Catching 6-1 San Francisco for the division is a stretch, but a wild card with double-digit wins is the most likely outcome.
swingFactors: Charles Cross's ankle and the line's pass protection
Week 12 at San Francisco for division hopes

confidence.note: Seven games split between two QBs. The defense is backed by last season, but the offense's true level is unclear.
